title: Sîtâbaldî inscription of the time of Vikramâditya VI. ; Śaka-Saṁvat 1008
html:
SITABALDI INSCRIPTION OF THE TIME OF VIKRAMADITYA VI.;
SAKA-SAMVAT 1008.

By F. KIELHORN, PH.D., LL.D., C.I.E.; GÖTTINGEN.

This inscription is on an elaborately sculptured pillar which was found by the late General Sir A. Cunningham at Sitábaldi, near Nágpur, in the Central Provinces, and is now in the Government Museum at Nágpur.7 To judge from the photograph before me, the sculptured part of the pillar measures about 5' high by 2½' broad, of which the inscription occupies the middle portion. Above the inscription is a row of small figures, and above these are, in the centre a linga, and on the two sides of it representations of the gods Brahmar and Vishnu; below the inscription are some cows and calves, and below these there is again a row of small figures, apparently fighting. I edit the inscription from an estampage, supplied to me some years ago by Dr. Fleet.

The inscription contains 11 lines of writing which covers a space of about 2' broad by 11' high, and is fairly well preserved. The size of the letters is about 1' in the upper lines, and rather less than ¾' in the lower ones. The characters are Nágarí. The language is very incorrect Sanskrit, and the whole is in prose. In respect of orthography, it will be sufficient to note that the consonant b, with perhaps one exception,8 is expressed by the sign for v, and that the dental sibilant is generally employed for the palatal, and the palatal once for the dental (in sahaśraváhu, l. 6). As regards grammar and lexicography, attention may especially be drawn to the Prákṛit termination9 u in saku, l. 1, dásu, l. 8, tatparu and dhavalu, l. 9, and dvádasu, l. 10; to the employment of the words chađaka, l. 5, and panatí, 'a great-grandson,' and nītí, 'a grandson,' l. 8, which must have been taken from the author's vernacular; and to the peculiar construction of the numerals in line 10.

Opening with the words 'ôm, may it be well,' and a date which will be considered below, the inscription (in lines 2-4) refers itself to the reign of victory of 'the refuge of the universe, the favourite of Fortune and of the Earth,' the Mahárájádhirája Paramésvara Paramabhaṭṭāraka, the glorious Tribhuvanamalladêva, the frontal ornament of the family of Satyáśraya and ornament of the Châlukyas, i.e. the king Vikramâditya VI. of the Western Châlukya dynasty.10 It then mentions (in lines 4-7), as a dependent of the king, the Mahásámanta11 Dhâdîbha[m]ðaka, also called the Ránaka Dhâdiadêva, who had emigrated from Latalaura, was born in the Mahârâshtrakûta lineage, and was distinguished by such titles as 'the scatterer of hostile armies, in war a Sahasrabâhu;12 a uterine brother of others' wives, the wrestler of all wrestlers, he who obtained favour by a boon of (the goddess) Châmundâ.' And in lines 7-10 the inscription records that a dependent of this Dhâdiadêva, the Danđanáyaka13 Vâsudêva, a son of the bhaṭta Padmanâbha, grandson of the bhaṭta [Bô]papai and great-grandson of the bhaṭta Viṭhapai, who belonged to the Kânya śâkhâ and Vatsa gôtra and hâd five pravaras, and who also had emigrated from Latalaura, 'a slave to cows and Brâhmanas' and ardent worshipper of the god Vishnu,14 who had obtained favour by a boon of (the god) Nârasinha (Vishnu), gave 12 nivartanas of land, which had been purchased by him, for the grazing of cattle; also 7 nivartanas for daily food given to cattle; and 5 nivartanas for vâhaka (?),15 apparently to a temple at which the inscription was put up. The concluding line 11 states that, whosoever appropriates the land so given, robs the gods Brahman, Vishnu and Mahêsvara (Śiva); and that, who steals the cows from it, falls into hell.

The inscription is dated, in lines 1-2, in Śaka-Samvat 1008, on Friday, the third lunar day of the bright half of Vaiśâkha of the year Prabhava. By the southern luni-solar system the year Prabhava would be Śaka-Samvat 1009, not 1008, expired; but the date does not work out satisfactorily for either year, nor for the four surrounding years. For the third tithi of the bright half of Vaiśâkha ended,—

in Śaka-Samvat 1006 expired, on Thursday, 11th April, A.D. 1084;
" " " 1007 expired, on Monday, 31st March, A.D. 1085;
" " " 1008 expired, on Sunday, 19th April, A.D. 1086;
" " " 1009 expired, on Thursday,16 8th April, A.D., 1087;
" " " 1010 expired, on Tuesday, 28th March, A.D. 1088; and Wednesday, 26th April, A.D. 1088;
" " " 1011 expired, on Monday, 16th April, A.D. 1089.

In my opinion, the day intended by the date is really Thursday, the 8th April, A.D. 1087, and the writer made a mistake in regard to the week-day.

The place Latalaura, which is twice mentioned in this inscription, I am unable to identify.

Footnotes

1(p. 304, n. 1) With this phrase, for the employment of which there was no reason here, compare rájávalí-púrvvam in Ind. Ant. Vol. VI. p. 191, line 1 of the inscription.

2(p. 304, n. 2) i.e. śréshthint.

3(p. 304, n. 3) The superscript line of ó is very faint in the estampage.

4(p. 304, n. 4) i.e. -prabhritayaḥ, for -prabhritibhiḥ.

5(p. 304, n. 5) Read -múrttir=.

6(p. 304, n. 6) i.e. sútradhára-.

7↩(p. 304, n. 7) See Archæol. Survey of India, Vol. VII. p. 142; and the Gazetteer of the Central Provinces, p. 341.

8↩(p. 304, n. 8) In the name Bópapai in line 8, if my reading of it is correct.

9↩(p. 304, n. 9) Compare Ind. Ant. Vol. XVI. p. 207.

10↩(p. 305, n. 1) See Dr. Fleet's Kanarese Dynasties, p. 48; and Dr. Bhandarkar's Early History of the Dekkan, p. 64.

11↩(p. 305, n. 2) i.e. 'the great feudatory.'

12↩(p. 305, n. 3) i.e. Arjuna.

13↩(p. 305, n. 4) i.e. 'one who applies the rod,' a head police-officer, etc.

14↩(p. 305, n. 5) The exact sense of the word ubhayadvâda[sô]dhavalu of the text is not apparent.

15↩(p. 305, n. 6) About the meaning of the word vâhaka also I am doubtful; perhaps it denotes here the drivers or attendants of the cattle.

16↩(p. 305, n. 7) On this day the third tithi of the bright half ended 16 h, 9 m. after mean sunrise.

17↩(p. 305, n. 8) From an impression, supplied to me by Dr. Fleet.

18↩(p. 305, n. 9) Expressed by a symbol.

19↩(p. 305, n. 10) The date would have been correctly expressed thus: Śakanripa-kâl-âtita-samvatsara-batêshu daśasv=ashṭ-âdhikêshu yatr=ânkatô=pi Śakê 1008 Prabhava-samvatsar-ântargata-Vaisâkha-suddha-tritiyâ-Sukradinê.

20↩(p. 305, n. 11) The aksharas lâ and ta, having been originally omitted, are engraved above the line.

21↩(p. 305, n. 12) This may possibly have been altered to ashṭâdhikê.

22↩(p. 305, n. 13) Here and in other places below, which it is unnecessary to point out separately, the rules of sandhi have not been observed.

23↩(p. 306, n. 1) Originally °râjyêh appears to have been engraved. The following sign of punctuation is superfluous.

24↩(p. 306, n. 2) Read -vinirggatô and -prasûtô.

25↩(p. 306, n. 3) This word chadaka is not Sanskrit; it probably is connected with the root chat, 'to break,' and apparently the whole biruda is equivalent to aribalanjshudana. Compare also the Marâthî chadaka, 'a slap, a stroke.'

26↩(p. 306, n. 4) Nâman is quite superfluous here; its sense is contained in the following samastarâjâvalî.

27↩(p. 306, n. 5) Read -rânakah; but the word in the whole phrase, beginning with tatpâdapadm-ôpajîvî in line 4, should really have been put in the Locative. The following sign of punctuation is again superfluous.

28↩(p. 306, n. 6) This word and the following words in the Nominative case, qualifying as they do Vâsudêvêna in line 9, should have been put in the Instrumental.

29↩(p. 306, n. 7) This sign of visarga was originally omitted.

30↩(p. 306, n. 8) Read -sâkhâyâm, or perhaps rather -sâkhtyô.

31↩(p. 306, n. 9) Read °rtyô.

32↩(p. 306, n. 10) Pañatî and nîttî in the following compound are clearly closely related to and synonymous with the Marâthî pañatû, 'great-grandson,' and nâtû, 'grandson;' the Sanskrit words would be pranaptâ and naptâ.

33↩(p. 306, n. 11) The first akshara of this name might also be read vvô or, perhaps, ghô; the last akshara was originally pau, but has been altered to pai.

34↩(p. 306, n. 12) Read -putrô.

35↩(p. 306, n. 13) On the termination u of this and of some of the following words see my remarks on page 304 above.

36↩(p. 306, n. 14) The akshara in brackets may possibly be syê. I do not understand the exact meaning of this compound; perhaps it has reference to religious observances on the 12th day (dvâdaâtî) of the two halves of the month.

37↩(p. 306, n. 15) Read Nârasimha38(p. 306, n. o) .

39↩(p. 306, n. 16) Intended for grihitâni bhûmi-nivarttanâni dvâdaśa. On the construction of the pumerals here and below compare Ind. Ant. Vol. XVI. p. 207.

40↩(p. 306, n. 17) Probably intended for êtâ bhûmayah pratipâditâh.

41↩(p. 306, n. 18) Read êtâ bhûmtr=yê lôpayanti tê Brahma-Vishnu-Mahêsvarâmîl=lôpayanti | êram yô gâ lôpayati sa kumbhipâkê patati ||
